cands.name: Rachel Grage
cands.bio: Democratic nominee, 55, biomedical engineer. Bachelor's and master's degrees in engineering from Tulane. Former elected president of her homeowners' association. Lost the 2024 Florida House District 16 race to Rep. Kiyan Michael with 39%. Won the Aug 2026 Democratic primary. Never held public office.
cands.local_ties: Born in Oswego, New York; moved to Florida in 2019 (Ballotpedia via search summary). Married to a physician and former Army medical officer; four children.

record.text: Priorities: affordable housing and insurance costs, public-school funding and teacher pay, small-business development (candidate questionnaire, News4JAX).
2024 nominee for Florida House District 16; lost to the incumbent Republican with 39% (Florida Trib, Oct 2024 coverage).

endorsements.text: Florida AFL-CIO and National Women's Political Caucus (per Wikipedia 2026 district page citing flaflcio.org and nwpc.org; not opened).

cands.gaps: Residence not stated in sources. Affiliations (Catholic Charities, Equality Florida, Democratic Women's Club) come from a Ballotpedia snippet and were left out of the bio. No fundraising/outside-money details.

cands.name: John H. Rutherford
cands.bio: Republican, 73. Jacksonville Sheriff's Office 1974-2003 (director of corrections), three terms as Jacksonville Sheriff 2003-2015, then elected to Congress in 2016; now in his fifth term. B.S. in criminology (Florida State) and FBI National Academy graduate. Sits on House Appropriations.
cands.local_ties: Born in Omaha, family moved to Jacksonville in the 1950s; married 53 years; member of Assumption Catholic Church. District: southeast Jacksonville and St. Johns County.

record.text: Sits on the House Appropriations Committee (subcommittees on Homeland Security; Military Construction-VA; Transportation-HUD, per Wikipedia's 118th list).
Sponsored the STOP School Violence Act (2018), authorizing $50 million a year in grants for training to prevent school gun violence; the House passed it 407-10.
Self-described priorities: border security, cost of living via tax and spending cuts, military installations, infrastructure and veterans' care.

controversies.text: Office of Congressional Ethics found 157 late stock-trade reports (Jan 2017-Dec 2021); he paid an $800 fine in Nov 2021 and the House Ethics Committee announced an investigation on May 31, 2022. Final outcome not found in sources.

endorsements.text: Donald Trump (Florida Politics, Feb 11, 2026; paywalled, not opened), AIPAC, NRA Political Victory Fund and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce (listed on the Wikipedia 2026 district page).

cands.gaps: Photo skipped per brief. Never served in the Florida Legislature, so no state votes. 119th-Congress committee list and outcome of the 2022 Ethics probe not verified. No 2026 outside-spending data found.

votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.
Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.
